Empathic, non-judgemental approach, including when discussing smoking.

Asks about smoking, diabetes and other risk factors for recurrent periductal infection.
Interpretation
Correctly identifies a breast abscess with a persisting underlying mass and skin changes in a non-breastfeeding woman, with failure to respond to antibiotics.
States that non-lactational abscess or mastitis is a red flag because it may be caused by, or may mask, an underlying carcinoma, including inflammatory breast cancer.
Identifies the features that raise suspicion of malignancy: residual firm irregular mass, peau d'orange, nipple retraction, axillary node, recurrence at same site, age over 40, family history.
Management
Assesses for sepsis and need for hospital referral (observations, systemic features, comorbidities) and decides she can be managed as an outpatient with close review.

kids.x: Age 35 or over, so ultrasound plus mammogram (bilateral mammogram, with axillary assessment).
Ultrasound to confirm and characterise the collection and the underlying mass.

check.x: Arranges imaging now, at presentation, not after the infection has settled:
Plans drainage of the abscess, with ultrasound-guided needle aspiration preferred, and sends pus for culture.

kids.x: Core biopsy (not FNA alone) of the residual solid mass and abscess wall.
Skin punch biopsy for the skin thickening or peau d'orange if inflammatory breast cancer is suspected.
Biopsy of any suspicious axillary node on ultrasound.

check.x: Plans tissue diagnosis:
Explains the triple assessment (clinical, imaging, non-operative tissue biopsy) and the rule that all three must be concordant before the lesion is called benign.
States that any discordance, or a persistent or recurrent lesion after treatment, needs further investigation and tissue diagnosis.
Antibiotics reviewed according to eTG, with culture results, as non-lactational infection often needs anaerobic cover; analgesia advised.
Urgent referral to a breast surgeon or breast clinic, and a review within 48 to 72 hours with a safety net.
Plans follow-up until the mass has fully resolved, with repeat imaging or biopsy if any mass remains after the infection clears.
Offers smoking cessation support and notes it as a risk factor for periductal mastitis and recurrence.
Communication
Uses plain language without jargon and checks understanding.

kids.x: Acknowledges her concern and her friend's experience.
Says that infection is the most likely cause but that cancer must be excluded; avoids false reassurance and avoids premature diagnosis of cancer.

check.x: Responds honestly to the patient's fear of cancer:
Explains why a mammogram and biopsy are needed even though this looks like an infection, and addresses her reluctance about tests.
Explains what drainage and biopsy involve, and what to expect from the next appointments.
Gives clear safety-netting: return or go to the Emergency Department for worsening pain, spreading redness, high fever, feeling unwell or rigors.
Summarises the plan, confirms the patient agrees and invites questions.

desc: This station involves taking a focused history from a woman with a red, painful breast lump who is not breastfeeding, planning her work-up and management, and counselling her about why imaging and biopsy are needed as well as treating the infection.
explain:
Why a non-lactational breast abscess is a red flag

Breast infection in a woman who is not breastfeeding is unusual. It may be periductal mastitis (strongly associated with smoking), but an infection can also be caused by, or can mask, an underlying carcinoma. Inflammatory breast cancer commonly mimics mastitis, with a red, warm, swollen breast, skin thickening and peau d'orange, and is often treated as an infection for weeks before it is recognised. Failure to respond to antibiotics, a residual mass, nipple retraction, an axillary node and recurrence in the same site all raise concern. In this case Helen is 46, has a family history, has a persistent underlying irregular mass and skin changes extending beyond the area of erythema, and has had a previous episode.

What must be done, and when

  • Image at presentation, not after the infection settles. At 35 or over this means ultrasound plus mammogram. Ultrasound defines the collection and the underlying mass, and also assesses the axilla.

  • Treat the infection: ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is preferred over incision and drainage, with pus sent for culture, and antibiotics chosen according to eTG (non-lactational infection often needs anaerobic cover).

  • Biopsy any residual mass, abscess wall or skin change. Core biopsy is preferred to FNA for a solid lesion. A skin punch biopsy is needed if inflammatory breast cancer is a possibility. Persistent or recurrent disease requires tissue diagnosis.

  • Refer urgently to a breast surgeon or breast clinic and review early (48 to 72 hours). Follow the patient until the mass has resolved completely.

Triple assessment

The three components are clinical assessment (history and examination of both breasts and axillae), imaging (age 35 or over: mammogram plus ultrasound; under 35: ultrasound first, with mammogram added selectively) and non-operative tissue biopsy (core biopsy preferred to FNA for solid lesions). The key rule is concordance: a lump can be called benign only if all three components agree. Any discordance, for example a benign-looking biopsy from a mass that is clinically or radiologically suspicious, needs further investigation, such as repeat or larger-volume biopsy, or excision.

Communication

Patients are often reluctant to have more tests when they have been told it is an infection. Explain honestly that infection is the most likely cause, but that the same signs can occur with cancer and that the only way to be certain is imaging and a biopsy. Avoid false reassurance, but also avoid telling her she has cancer before the results are available. Support smoking cessation and give clear safety-net advice.
focus: Breast lump and breast abscess work-up
guide:
A high-performing candidate would take a focused history that establishes the lump is non-lactational, recognise the abscess with an underlying mass and skin changes as a red flag, and clearly state that malignancy including inflammatory breast cancer must be excluded. They would plan ultrasound and mammogram now, drainage with culture, and core biopsy of the residual mass and any skin change, and explain the concordance rule of triple assessment. They would refer urgently, arrange early review and follow-up until the mass is gone, and counsel the patient honestly and empathically.

A borderline candidate would treat this as simple mastitis, change the antibiotic and arrange review, without imaging or biopsy, or would defer imaging until after the infection has resolved. They would not recognise the significance of the residual mass and the skin changes, and would give false reassurance when asked about cancer.
patient:
Profile:

  • Name: Helen Marchetti

  • Age: 46-years-old

  • Gender: Female

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: No

  • Setting: General Practice clinic

Presenting complaint: Painful, red lump in the left breast.

History of presenting complaint (give only if asked):

  • Ten days ago you noticed a tender area near the left nipple. It has become a firm, red, painful lump.

  • You saw a locum GP five days ago, who said it was mastitis and gave you flucloxacillin 500 mg four times a day. You have taken every dose. The redness is a bit better but the lump is still there and feels hard. It has not shrunk. You are worried about it.

  • You have had fevers and sweats on and off for four days. You feel tired.

  • You are not breastfeeding. Your youngest child is 12 and you last breastfed 11 years ago. You are not pregnant (periods are regular, last period 2 weeks ago).

  • No nipple discharge. The left nipple has been slightly pulled in for about a month; you thought it was nothing. No trauma, piercings or recent breast procedures.

  • You have had a similar, smaller sore area near the same nipple 18 months ago, which settled with antibiotics. No imaging was done.

  • No weight loss, night sweats, bone pain, cough or headaches.

Medical history: Nil significant. No diabetes. No previous breast biopsies. Never had a mammogram.

Medications: Flucloxacillin as above. No hormonal contraception or HRT. No known drug allergies.

Family history: Your mother had breast cancer at age 58. No known BRCA gene testing. No ovarian cancer.

Social history: Smoker, 15 cigarettes a day for 25 years. Alcohol 2 standard drinks on weekends. Married, works as a primary school teacher.

Cues and questions to ask:

  • Early on say: “I just want this infection gone. I haven't got time for lots of tests.”

  • Ask: “A friend of mine was told she had mastitis and it turned out to be cancer. Could that be what this is?” (Be reassured if the candidate is honest and explains clearly, without false reassurance or alarm.)

  • Ask: “Why do I need a mammogram if it's an infection?”

  • Ask: “Will I need a needle in it, or an operation?”

  • Agree to the plan if it is explained clearly, including attending the scans and returning for review.

Examiner findings (provide to the candidate after the history):

  1. Left breast: 4 cm tender, warm, erythematous area in the upper outer quadrant adjacent to the areola, with a fluctuant centre.

  2. A separate firm, irregular, non-tender area about 2 cm across, deep to the abscess, which does not feel cystic.

  3. Skin thickening and mild peau d'orange over the lateral breast, extending beyond the area of erythema.

  4. Left nipple is mildly retracted. No discharge.

  5. One tender, mobile 1 cm left axillary lymph node. Right breast and right axilla normal. Supraclavicular fossae clear.
points: Non-lactational breast abscess or mastitis is a red flag for underlying carcinoma, including inflammatory breast cancer, and needs imaging at presentation as well as treatment of the infection.
Women aged 35 or over need ultrasound plus mammogram; under 35, ultrasound first with selective mammogram.
Biopsy (core preferred over FNA) any residual mass, abscess wall or skin change; persistent or recurrent disease needs tissue diagnosis.
Triple assessment is clinical, imaging and non-operative biopsy, and all three must be concordant before a lump is called benign.
Follow the patient until the mass has completely resolved and do not give false reassurance.

stem:
You are a final-year medical student on a General Practice placement. Helen Marchetti, a 46-year-old woman, has come to the clinic with a painful, red lump in her left breast. She was seen by a locum GP five days ago, diagnosed with mastitis and started on oral flucloxacillin. She has returned because the lump is not settling.

Her observations today are: temperature 37.9 °C, heart rate 92/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mrs Marchetti (3 minutes).
Interpret the examination findings given by the examiner and outline your investigation and management plan to the examiner (2 minutes).
Explain to Mrs Marchetti what you think is happening and what will happen next (3 minutes).
